title: Mathematics or the Verifier? A Null Result for One Verifier-Filtered Self-Training Recipe on a 1.5B Model

paragraphs.text: # Mathematics or the Verifier? A Null Result for One Verifier-Filtered Self-Training Recipe on a 1.5B Model

Mathematics or the Veriﬁer? A Null Result for
One Veriﬁer-Filtered Self-Training Recipe on a
1.5B Model
Tan Sang Nguyen1 and Duy Anh Tran1
Ton Duc Thang University, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam
52300057@student.tdtu.edu.vn, 52300006@student.tdtu.edu.vn
Abstract. Self-training and reinforcement learning with veriﬁable re-
wards report large gains for small language models, but a rising score
does not show that a model learned mathematics rather than what its
veriﬁer accepts. We study the cheapest form of the loop, generate–verify–
select–train with oﬄine LoRA SFT, on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with the
rule-based veriﬁer math-verify, on held-out MATH-500 and GSM8K ex-
ams (150 problems; 500 in a ﬁnal round) at four learning rates on MATH-
500 and two on GSM8K. No pass@1 or pass@k gain has a problem-level
bootstrap interval excluding zero; in the ﬁnal round, with a revised (not
validated) recipe, pass@1 falls 3.2–4.8 points in each of three seeds (mean
−4.1; two of three intervals exclude zero). The design detects only gains
of about 10 points of pass@1 (6 in the ﬁnal round; 80% power, inter-
vals without seed variance, so likely more). A positive gate fails: training
on reference solutions lowers pass@1 by 32.2 points, which we did not
diagnose (a pipeline defect would also produce it), so the null concerns
this recipe only and cannot show that self-training fails. Accuracies are
graded by the veriﬁer that selects the data (the ﬁnal round also by a
string-match grader), so neither the mathematics nor the veriﬁer ques-
tion is answered. As a post hoc audit we track the share of the loop’s
own correct solutions that a storage defect in our pipeline rejects (about
one in six). It falls by 1.5–2.6 points with intervals reaching zero; this fall
is tied to the falling \boxed share by an identity, so it is no evidence of
adaptation. Two injected-bias runs, one whose rule is visible in the gold
answer, show no selective avoidance but are not valid positive controls
(one cannot elicit avoidance by construction, the other is a single run
without rt), so the audit is uninformative about adaptation. Two con-
trols, patching a rarer defect and removing the ﬁlter, show no consistent
diﬀerence (no ﬁlter is lower on pass@k, at 3–4× the dose) but are dose-
confounded or too small to detect one. Scores before the ﬁnal round use
the veriﬁer with the defect.
Keywords: self-training · self-improvement · veriﬁer bias · mathe-
matical reasoning · small language models · veriﬁable rewards · null
result.

1
Introduction
A common recipe for improving the mathematical reasoning of a small lan-
guage model (SLM) without human annotation is to let the model generate its
own solutions, keep those an automated veriﬁer judges correct, and ﬁne-tune on
them, for several rounds. We call this the Generate–Verify–Train (GVT) loop;
it underlies STaR [19], ReST [12], ReST-EM [11] and rejection-sampling ﬁne-
tuning [17]. But the veriﬁer never reads the reasoning: a rule-based veriﬁer such
as math-verify1 only extracts a ﬁnal answer and compares it with the gold, and
it rejects some correct answers written in forms it does not parse (Section 3.2).
The training signal is “was the ﬁnal string accepted”, not “were the steps right”.
The same gap runs through reinforcement learning with veriﬁable rewards
(RLVR), which reports large gains at this scale [14,3,20], though only 8.6 of one
study’s 37.6 points lie beyond format correction. Shao et al. [9] ﬁnd that GRPO
with random rewards raises Qwen2.5-Math-7B by 21.4 points on MATH-500,
against 29.1 with ground-truth rewards. A rising score therefore does not by itself
show that a model has learned to solve more problems, rather than to surface
behaviour it already had or to produce what its reward accepts. In RLVR, per-
step false-negative rates on the policy’s own rollouts have been tracked [4,16];
we study the question in a cheap and common form of the loop, oﬄine rejection-
sampling SFT, where a false reject removes a training example (and, if bound to
a problem, the problem), and apply a per-round false-reject measurement there,
post hoc, for one defect of our pipeline.
We ask: after several GVT rounds, is the model better at mathematics, or
has it only learned to write what the veriﬁer accepts? We ﬁxed four measures
in advance: (i) pass@1; (ii) pass@k; (iii) output style, chieﬂy the share of gen-
erations containing \boxed; and (iv) per-problem transitions (problems added
and lost between rounds). The pre-set reading rule was that “learning the ver-
iﬁer’s style” requires pass@1 to rise, pass@k to stay ﬂat and style to converge
at once. In hindsight the rule is one-sided: it can only ﬁre when accuracy rises
(Section 5.1). The higher learning rates, the controls, the round count and k
at those rates, sample accuracy as primary measure, the termination measures
and the re-scoring for a second veriﬁer defect, and the ﬁnal 500-problem round
(Section 4.6) were all added after seeing earlier runs; all are post hoc.
We detect no improvement at any learning rate, though gains below about 10
points of pass@1 or 3.5–5.5 of sample accuracy could have been missed (intervals
omit training-seed variance), and no arm of this recipe improves, so the result
concerns the recipe. The second branch is untested: no run varies the frequent
veriﬁer defect, scores are graded by the selecting veriﬁer (one string-match check
on the ﬁnal round), and the post hoc audit of Section 5.3 is uninformative about
adaptation. What appears, most clearly at the highest rate, is lower accuracy
on the solutions the model does ﬁnish, though on one seed the cap share carries
more of it (Section 4.5). A sharp pooled decline is absent in the isolated runs at

10−5, which train on about 4.5× fewer examples (Section 4.1); dose and pooling
are confounded.
Contributions.
– For a 1.5B model, LoRA SFT and one rule-based veriﬁer, no gain is de-
tectable on a held-out exam at any learning rate we tried (a coarse grid that
also changes k and rounds), with bootstrap intervals and the smallest eﬀects
the design could detect. No arm improves, not even training on reference
solutions, so this is a null for the recipe, not a statement about self-training.
– A post hoc per-round false-reject audit of one veriﬁer defect (the RLVR
tracking [4,16] applied to oﬄine SFT; not a novel method). The rejected
share falls by 1.5–2.6 points with intervals reaching zero, tied to the falling
\boxed share by an identity; the audit is uninformative about adaptation
(Section 5.3).
– A decomposition of an accuracy decline under a ﬁxed token cap into a
ﬁnished-accuracy part and a cap-share part: at the highest rate, ﬁnished
generations lose 5.5–10.6 points against the untrained model on the same
problem mix (A, B and no-ﬁlter runs; train-on-gold loses about 26), and the
cap-hit share rises only at that rate.
2
Related Work
Self-training and its limits. STaR [19] introduced the generate–ﬁlter–retrain
loop, and ReST [12], ReST-EM [11] and RFT [17] formalise it; ReST-EM, which
like us restarts from the base model each iteration, reports diminishing gains
after the ﬁrst round. Yue et al. [18] show that RL raises pass@1 while the base
model wins at large pass@k, and Teacher-Free Self-Training [13] concludes that
self-training “ampliﬁes but does not compound”. Training repeatedly on model-
generated data erodes distribution tails [10], and a narrow selector can accelerate
collapse [8].
RL with veriﬁable rewards at small scale. RLVR with GRPO reports large gains
near our model size: one training example lifts Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B on MATH-
500 from 36.0% to 73.6% [14], 7,000 examples lift DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-
1.5B on AMC23 from 63% to 80% [3], and zero-RL works on open base models
from 0.5B [20]. These studies improve accuracy, which our SFT loop does not;
of Wang et al.’s 37.6 points only 8.6 lie beyond format correction. Shao et al. [9]
show that it need not be reward learning (random rewards also help, via ampliﬁed
pre-existing behaviour). We do not compete with RLVR on accuracy; the audit
of Section 5.3 asks whether a loop has adapted to one veriﬁer defect, and we
apply it only to SFT.
Veriﬁer error. TinyV [16] ﬁnds that rule-based veriﬁers reject many correct
solutions; From Accuracy to Robustness [6] reports an average recall of 86%,
and 0.95 for math-verify on their MATH subset. Imperfect Veriﬁers [1] models

ﬁxed false-accept and false-reject rates. Egashira et al. [4] ﬁnd in RLVR that
systematic false negatives behave like random noise whereas false positives can
cause plateau or collapse. For format-based false negatives they see the policy
ﬁrst unlearn the triggering behaviour. Our setting diﬀers in paradigm (oﬄine
SFT with a fresh adapter per round) and task, and our controls cannot test
their ﬁndings (Section 4.3).
Auditing self-improvement. Xu et al. [15] audit LoRA self-training of Qwen3-
8B against a frozen control and identify seven measurement failures, including
training-seed variance and a ﬁxed token cap under style drift, that each invert
a ﬁnding when uncontrolled. This is the study closest to ours; it is why we
separate ﬁnished accuracy from termination (Section 4.5). We diﬀer in scale (a
1.5B model), in the veriﬁer (a rule-based one whose rejection defect we measured)
and in auditing what that veriﬁer’s ﬁltering does to the training pool, not only
whether accuracy moved. Kim et al. [7] show that self-distillation with a teacher
that sees the solution can cut accuracy; our train-on-gold drop resembles this, but
we did not test its cause (Section 4.6). Our per-round false-reject measurement
(Section 5.3) is not new (it is the per-step tracking of Egashira et al. and TinyV,
applied to oﬄine SFT and to a defect of our own pipeline), and we claim neither
it nor the patch control as a contribution. Supplementary Appendix A gives the
full comparison.
3
Setup
3.1
The GVT Loop
Each round t has four steps. Generate: the current model samples k solutions per
problem. Verify: math-verify extracts the ﬁnal answer and compares it with the
gold. Select: accepted solutions are kept. Train: a fresh LoRA adapter is attached
to the base model and trained on the kept solutions for one epoch. Round 0 is
the untrained base model; the round-t model (t ≥1) is the base plus an adapter
trained on the pool accepted at round t −1. Adapters are not accumulated, so
earlier rounds aﬀect later ones only through the data they generate; conclusions
about (non-)compounding below apply to this restart-from-base design, which
gives compounding less room than continued training would.
3.2
The Veriﬁer and Its Directional Bias
A format probe that re-renders gold answers in individually valid forms shows
that \dfrac/\tfrac are rejected 100% of the time on both datasets (the com-
mand is not parsed). On real solutions (one public Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct solution
per problem for 200 MATH-500 problems, judged correct by a scripted nor-
malised comparison) the false-negative rate is 7.8% (10 of 128; Wilson interval
4.3–13.8%) on MATH-500 and 0% on GSM8K. Eight of the ten fail when the
whole solution is veriﬁed but pass when only the boxed answer is; most are com-
pound answers, so they are probably largely the gold-storage defect described

Mathematics or the Veriﬁer?
5
below rather than extraction of a wrong token. The audit inspected only rejec-
tions, so it gives no false-positive rate. The veriﬁer also cannot parse 51 of the
500 stored MATH-500 golds (10.2%); under V these problems always count as
unsolved and can never enter the training pool (V ′ makes 46 of them parseable
for boxed predictions). The oﬀset cancels in within-run diﬀerences only if those
problems would not otherwise change, which we did not check, and not in ratios
or levels across partitions (11–18 such problems per exam partition).
The patch. For the control we rewrote \dfrac and \tfrac to \frac before
parsing, removing the 100%-rejection class and nothing else.
The gold-storage defect (post hoc). Our pipeline stores the gold without a de-
limiter, and math-verify applies its full LATEX extraction only inside \boxed{}
or $...$, so a correct boxed prediction can fail against a bare gold (e.g. the
prediction \boxed{\frac{4}{3}} against the stored gold \frac43). Re-scoring
the saved generations with a veriﬁer V ′ that wraps the gold in \boxed{} when
the prediction contains one shows that this defect rejects 15.5–18.3% of the gen-
erations V ′ accepts. It would enlarge the round-0 kept pool by about a ﬁfth to
a quarter (440 →542, +23%; this pool covers only the 350 selection problems,
so its 18.8% rejected share diﬀers from the 15.5–18.3% over all 500), against 0–4
examples for the \dfrac patch, and it lowers absolute pass@1 by 4.7–8.0 points
in self-training. It is bound to the problem, not to the answer: on the 54–62
problems where it ever ﬁres, it rejects 94–98% of correct answers in every round
(87–98% where V parses the gold), and 29–34 of these problems have a gold the
original veriﬁer cannot parse at all, so no answer form avoids it there. Re-scored,
sample accuracy still falls in all ﬁve runs we re-scored (three self-training, two
train-on-gold); the original-veriﬁer changes are 0.73–0.85 of the re-scored ones,
an observed ratio that we do not use to rescale other numbers or intervals. All
tables keep the original veriﬁer, the one the loop trained with. Section 5.3 uses
this defect for the adaptation audit; Supplementary Appendix B gives the full
analysis.
3.3
Two Experimental Designs
Design P (pooled) loads both datasets (500 problems each) together and trains
one adapter per round on the union of accepted solutions, with selection and
evaluation on the same 1,000 problems. Design I (isolated) uses one dataset and
one adapter per run, and holds out 30% of the 500 problems (150) as an exam
set; generation runs on all 500 problems each round, but only the other 350 can
enter the training pool, and all Design I pass rates are on the exam set. Table S1
summarises them.
Design I has three runs, all Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, ﬁve rounds, k = 8, diﬀer-
ing in one respect each: Run A (MATH-500, original veriﬁer), Run B (MATH-
500, patched veriﬁer) and Run C (GSM8K, original veriﬁer). Runs A and B were
repeated at a second seed; since the seed also sets the train/exam partition, the
repetition draws a diﬀerent 150-problem exam set. Most of the later evidence
comes from higher-rate runs introduced in Section 4.4; Table S4 (Supplementary
Appendix E) lists every run. A “seed” sets the exam partition, the selection set

and the training randomness at once; runs with the same seed share the par-
tition. “Five rounds” means round 0 (the untrained model) and four adapters,
each trained once on the previous round’s pool; “three rounds” means round 0
and two adapters, so the round-2 model is a single adapter (about 195 optimizer
steps for Run A at 5×10−4) trained on the round-1 pool. All runs use one model
family, Qwen2.5.
3.4
Models, Data, Training, Metrics
We use Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (Design P uses both,
Design I the 1.5B model only) and the ﬁrst 500 problems of the GSM8K test
split [2] and MATH-500, the 500-problem subset of MATH [5]. The prompt is
a single user turn in the model’s chat template: “Solve the math problem. Put
the ﬁnal answer in \boxed{}.” followed by the problem. Generation samples at
temperature 0.8 with a cap of 512 new tokens; the other decoding settings come
from the checkpoint’s generation conﬁguration (top-p 0.8, top-k 20, repetition
penalty 1.1). Training is LoRA SFT (transformers 5.0.0, peft 0.19.1, TRL
1.10.0 SFTTrainer; rank 16, α = 32, on q_proj and v_proj, LoRA dropout
0, weight decay 0, gradient clipping 1.0 and trainer seed 42, all library defaults
read from the pinned sources; batch size 2, no accumulation; one epoch; AdamW
with linear learning-rate decay and no warmup; Python and torch seeds set
from the run seed; loss over the whole chat sequence, prompt included; fp16 on
one Kaggle T4), with a training sequence limit of 512 tokens that includes the
prompt. Because this limit equals the generation cap but also holds the prompt,
any kept solution longer than about 512 tokens minus the prompt length is cut
in training and loses its ﬁnal answer and end-of-sequence token (24–26% of the
round-0 pool; Section 4.5). All kept solutions are used, so the number of optimizer
steps per round is half the pool size. The learning rate is 10−5 unless stated
otherwise; this value was the default of our training code and was not tuned
(Section 4.4). Metrics per round, on the exam set: pass@1 is the correctness
of the ﬁrst of the k samples (one draw per problem, so it carries sampling
noise); pass@k; sample accuracy, the mean over all k samples; style counts over
all generations (boxed, dfrac, dollar, . . . ); and per-problem added/lost counts
between consecutive rounds, where a problem is solved in a round if at least one
of its k samples is accepted. Added minus lost therefore equals 150×∆pass@k, so
these counts add only the gross churn behind the net change, not an independent
test. pass@1 was ﬁxed in advance; sample accuracy was not among the pre-
set measures, but it estimates the same quantity from all k samples with less
variance, so after the runs we chose it as the primary accuracy measure. Claims
that rest on it, including the 2.2-point bound, are therefore post hoc in the choice
of measure. “Correct” always means accepted by the veriﬁer (preset reward), the
same veriﬁer that selects the training data.
Uncertainty. For every within-run change (round 0 against the last round) and
every paired comparison of two runs on the same exam partition we report a
95% interval from a paired problem-level bootstrap (10,000 resamples of the

7
150 exam problems; 2,000 for the matched and audit columns), which respects
the clustering of the k samples within a problem. These intervals do not cover
training-seed variance, which we see only across two or three seeds: the replicate
pair we use as a gauge ends 3.2 points of sample accuracy apart (a seed also
changes the exam partition, so such pairs mix training and partition variance).
We make no multiplicity correction and the runs are not independent (they share
exam partitions and round-0 draws), so patterns across runs are descriptive, not
tests; we apply the same reading to declines and to gains. Single proportions use
Wilson intervals. Detectable eﬀects. From the interval half-widths h in Table 2,
a change would be detected with 80% power at the 5% level only if it exceeded
about 2.8 h/1.96: about 10 points of pass@1, 8–10 of pass@k and 3.5–5.5 of
sample accuracy on MATH-500. Because h omits training-seed variance (the
replicate pair diﬀers by 3.2 points and B minus A ﬂips from +5.3 to −7.3 on
near-identical pools, Section 4.4), these are optimistic thresholds, not bounds:
even with h as the whole error, a gain at that size is missed 20% of the time,
and probably more often (Supplementary Appendix C).
4
Results
4.1
Design P: An Apparent Collapse
In the pooled design the 1.5B model declines severely and with acceleration
(pass@1 50.0% →18.6%, pass@8 72.6% →48.6%; Table S3, Supplementary
Appendix D), on both datasets (Table S2); the 0.5B decline is small. The ac-
cepted pool contracts every round and \boxed{} falls from 5,608 to 2,693 of
8,000 generations. This design cannot be read causally: one adapter trains on
both datasets’ pools, it scores on the problems it selects from, and it trains on
about 4.5× as many examples per round as the isolated MATH-500 run (3,962
against 872 at round 0); no run separates these (Supplementary Appendix D).
4.2
Design I at 10−5: Small Declines, a Larger One on GSM8K
On the held-out exam (Fig. S1 and Table S5 in Supplementary Appendix E)
pass@8 ends within 4 points of round 0 in every run. On MATH-500, pass@1
is 2.7–4.0 points lower at round 4, with every interval including zero (Table 2);
sample accuracy falls 1.2–3.2 points, with an interval excluding zero only for B
at seed 0 (A at seed 0 reaches 0.0), and matched ﬁnished accuracy 1.1–4.2, with
intervals that only just exclude zero for A and B at seed 0, which are close to one
replicate. We read this as a possible small decline, not an established one; what
we do not see is a gain of the size the design could detect. Run C (GSM8K)
declines more: pass@1 falls 12.7 points ([−21.3, −4.0]), almost all in ﬁnished
accuracy, but it took about twice Run A’s optimizer steps, so we do not attribute
this to the dataset alone. Length and cap-hit share barely change on MATH-500,
weak evidence that the adapter did little (Supplementary Appendix E).

4.3
The Patch Control Could Not Detect an Eﬀect
Runs A and B diﬀer only in the \dfrac/\tfrac patch. At round 4, B minus A
is −0.7 [−3.3, +2.0] points of pass@1 at seed 0 and +0.0 [−2.7, +2.7] at seed 1
(recomputed from the saved generations; Table 2 lists run-log values, −0.7 at
seed 1). This null is uninformative: \dfrac appears in 0.50–0.73% of generations,
so the kept pools diﬀer by 3–4 examples (under 0.5% of the 872-example pool),
and at 10−5 the adapter changes the outputs little anyway, so a null is what
prevalence alone predicts; the frequent gold-storage defect is in both arms.
4.4
Higher Learning Rates
Because 10−5 changed the MATH-500 outputs little, we reran Run A at 10−4
(three seeds), 2×10−4 (two) and 5×10−4 (two, with Run B), with three rounds
and k = 4 (Table 1). These runs diﬀer from the 10−5 runs in k, rounds, pool
size and the pass@k metric as well as rate, so only 10−4 to 5 × 10−4 isolates the
rate. At 5 × 10−4 every A/B run declines: pass@1 falls 4.0–11.3 points and the
sample-accuracy intervals exclude zero in all four A/B runs, though same-seed
A and B are closer to two replicates than four. The decline may grow with the
rate on one seed (sample-accuracy changes at 10−5 and 10−4 are similar, −1.2 to
−3.2 and −1.0 to −3.7): at seed 1 sample accuracy falls 1.5, 3.5 and 8.3 points
across the three rates, at seed 2 an almost ﬂat 3.7, 3.8 and 4.7. The cap-hit
share rises only at 5 × 10−4. The patch has no consistent eﬀect: B minus A in
round-2 pass@1 is +5.3 at seed 1 and −7.3 [−14.0, −0.7] at seed 2, a sign ﬂip
from pools diﬀering by 0–3 examples: trajectory noise. Style does not separate
imitation from drift: boxed share falls with the pool, which both would produce,
and the no-ﬁlter and gold arms decline with no veriﬁer in the selection step (they
are still scored by it), so generic SFT damage ﬁts as well.

Anatomy of the Decline
This subsection is post hoc and descriptive. Sample accuracy mixes whether a
ﬁnished solution is right with whether the model ﬁnishes within the 512-token
cap at all. Re-tokenising the saved text, we call a generation cap-hit at ≥508
tokens. At the rates where the share does not rise, 40–46% of round-2 MATH-500
generations already hit the cap (Table 1), so the cap binds from the start. At
5×10−4, compared with the untrained model on the same problem mix, ﬁnished
generations lose 5.5–10.6 points, with intervals excluding zero in ﬁve of six runs
(the six include two same-seed A/B pairs, which are close to replicates), while
the cap-hit share rises 2–14 points. The matched measure conditions on which
problems ﬁnish after training, so it is descriptive. A three-part decomposition
attributes 12–30% of the decline to the cap share in the three original seed-1
runs (and −2 and 5% in two further runs) and 52–72% at seed 2 (Table S9,
Supplementary Appendix H). At 10−4 and 2 × 10−4 the cap-hit share does not
rise and ﬁnished accuracy carries the whole change. Train-on-gold is diﬀerent:
responses shorten by more than half and ﬁnished accuracy collapses. Retraining
without truncated examples, or re-scoring at a 1,536-token cap, leaves the deﬁcit
in place (Supplementary Appendix H).

5
Discussion
5.1
Answer to the Research Question
Does the model get better at mathematics? Not detectably. No run raises pass@1
or pass@k with an interval excluding zero, at any rate; in the 500-problem ﬁnal
round pass@1 falls 3.2–4.8 points in each of three seeds. The sample-accuracy
ﬁgure of about 2.2 points is the largest upper limit among observed intervals, a
post hoc ﬁgure that omits seed variance, not a power statement; on the pre-set
measures the design could detect only about 10 points of pass@1 and 8–10 of
pass@k (6 and 5 in the ﬁnal round). Because no arm improves and the positive
gate failed, the null belongs to this recipe, and the study cannot say whether
self-training in general helps. Every score except the ﬁnal-round check below
is graded by the veriﬁer that selects the data (re-scoring ﬁve runs, three self-
training and two train-on-gold, with V ′ leaves the decline in place, Section 3).
On the ﬁnal-round generations a second grader (normalised string match of the
last \boxed against the gold, no math-verify; indep_grade.py) gives pass@1
changes of −3.6, −2.2, −4.6 for the three seeds (−30.0 for the gold arm) and
sample-accuracy changes of −2.5, −5.5, −5.3 (same sign and size). It reads only
the last \boxed, so a falling boxed share lowers both graders, and it does not
rule out a format artefact in the gate. Earlier runs are not independently graded.
Does it learn to write what the veriﬁer accepts? The data cannot settle this.
The pre-set pattern requires pass@1 to rise, which never happens detectably
(largest rise +0.7 [−6.7, +8.0]), so its silence is no evidence either way; no run
varies the frequent gold-storage defect, and the audit of Section 5.3 is too weak.
5.2
Interpretation
One explanation of the Design P curves is a self-reinforcing shrinking pool shaped
by the biased veriﬁer. The data neither support nor rule it out: the patch tests

Limitations
Unequal training doses confound every cross-arm comparison, and the controls
are underpowered: the patch changes 0–4 training examples, and the no-ﬁlter
and train-on-gold controls have two seeds each. Intervals cover only problem
draw and sampling, not training-seed variance; the ﬁnal-round loop has three
seeds, the gate and the bias controls one, and no multiplicity correction is ap-
plied. The learning-rate grid is coarse and changes k, rounds and dose with the
rate. Power is limited (about 10 points of pass@1 with 150 exam problems,
about 6 in Section 4.6). The adaptation audit is weak: 24–28 problems, 2–12
avoidance examples per round, and no valid positive control. The ﬁnal-round
loop has no no-ﬁlter arm. The veriﬁer audit used other models’ solutions and
inspected only rejections; the gold-storage defect ran unvaried through every
earlier run, whose headline numbers are graded by the biased veriﬁer that also
selects the data, and the ﬁnal-round string-match grader shares the \boxed de-
pendence. The ﬁnal-round decline and the gate failure cannot be attributed to

any single recipe change. Truncation: the 512-token cap binds from the start (a
quarter of the pool is cut). Scope: one model family and size, all instruction-
tuned (no base model), one veriﬁer, a restart-from-base design that leaves com-
pounding little room (no continued training), possible Qwen2.5 contamination
on MATH/GSM8K (unquantiﬁed), and a default repetition penalty (1.1) that
may depress the baseline.
7
Conclusion
We asked whether generate–verify–select–train iterations make a 1.5B model
better at mathematics or only teach it to write what a rule-based veriﬁer accepts.
The design detected no pass@1 or pass@k gain at any rate (it could see only gains
of about 10 and 8–10 points; 6 in a ﬁnal 500-problem round, where pass@1 falls
3.2–4.8 points in all three seeds). Because training on reference solutions lowers
pass@1 by about 30 points even with a revised recipe, this is a null for the recipe
and says little about self-training, and since scores are graded by the selecting
veriﬁer (apart from one string-match check), neither branch of the question is
answered. The post hoc false-reject audit is uninformative about adaptation:
its fall is tied to the falling \boxed share by an identity, and it has little power
(about 25 aﬀected problems, a handful of avoidance examples per round, no valid
positive control). At the highest rate the model is less accurate on the solutions
it ﬁnishes. The pooled design’s decline is absent in the isolated runs at 10−5,
which use about 4.5× fewer examples, so dose and pooling are confounded.
A dose-matched control for the gold-storage defect, a recipe that passes the
positive gate, and a second grader come ﬁrst (Supplementary Appendix K).

openaireview__claude.overall_feedback: The paper is honest about its limits and its arithmetic largely checks out (t-intervals, detectable-effect formula, Table 1 vs Table 3, the r_t identity). The core problem is that the positive gate fails and appears confounded with the \boxed dependence of both graders, so the 'null for the recipe' is inconclusive and the power statements are optimistic. The final round also shows a consistent decline that matches the boxed-share drop, which sits awkwardly under the 'null' label, and seven simultaneous recipe changes prevent attribution. Remaining issues are mostly framing and small internal inconsistencies, which are fixable in the text; a valid positive control would need new experiments.

comments.title: Failed positive gate leaves the null inconclusive for the recipe
comments.quote: gate failed, the null belongs to this recipe
comments.explanation:
A positive control that fails shows that the experiment cannot discriminate a gain from no gain; the logical consequence is that the null is uninformative about the recipe, not that it is a finding about the recipe. The paper's own gate text says the recipe 'cannot be called corrected' and the failure may be a pipeline defect. If the pipeline is defective, the loop's null inherits that defect. Scoping the claim to 'this recipe' then converts an inconclusive experiment into a recipe-specific negative. The scope restriction is a hedge on generality, not a licence to call the result a null for the recipe; the title 'A Null Result for One Recipe' presupposes that the recipe was fairly tested.

Also raised: Failed positive gate removes the meaning of both the null and the power statement | Contribution claim 'No arm improves ... so this is a null for the recipe' conflates a failed gate with evidence about the recipe | Failed positive gate turns the 'null' into an inconclusive result; Conclusion is firmer than Section 4.6 | Gate failure may be a measurement artefact, undermining 'null for the recipe'

comments.title: Gate collapse is plausibly a \boxed/grader artefact, not evidence about the recipe
comments.quote: That style carries no \boxed answer, which both graders read,
comments.explanation:
The prompt requires \boxed; the gold arm teaches $-delimited reference style with no \boxed, and both graders only read \boxed. A model trained this way scores near zero regardless of mathematical competence, so the -32 point 'collapse' may simply be unscorable output (the authors note both graders depend on \boxed but do not grade by last $-span / last number). Separately, off-policy terse reference solutions are not expected to raise accuracy of an already-instruction-tuned model (the cited Kim et al. result is that such SFT can lower it), whereas the loop trains on on-policy samples; so the gate may not be a positive control for the loop at all. In either case the failed gate does not bear on whether the self-generated-data arm could help, and the 'recipe passes if gate passes' criterion is unjustified. Earlier 1e-5/k=8 runs (Table 2, the bulk of the evidence) never had a gate at their settings; the 5e-4 gold arms came with different loss/targets.

Also raised: Gate confounded with grader: reference-style outputs carry no \boxed and both graders read \boxed | Gate failure is probably a measurement/format artefact, so it neither validates nor refutes the recipe | Gate and train-on-gold collapse may be a grader artefact; earlier 'unlikely verifier error' claim contradicts 4.6

Also raised: Gold-arm r_t rise is hard to reconcile with the stated identity and the 'no boxed answer' explanation | Gate-failure explanation conflicts with the earlier gold-arm boxed statistic and is untested

comments.title: Final-round loop decline matches the boxed-share drop; the 'independent' grader shares the \boxed dependence
comments.quote:
It reads only
the last \boxed, so a falling boxed share lowers both graders, and it does not
rule out a format artefact in the gate.
comments.explanation:
Section 5.3 reports boxed-share falls of roughly 3-5 points in the same recipe (-3.7, -2.7, -5.5 for the unbiased seeds), which is the same size as the pass@1 (-3.2 to -4.8) and sample-accuracy (-2.9 to -5.4) declines. Since correct answers without \boxed score zero under both graders, the whole decline could be produced by a format shift rather than any change in mathematics, and the paper's own identity makes this explicit for r_t. The 'independent' string-match grader adds no independence on this axis (same \boxed extraction, same gold normalisation, same generations); its agreement (-3.6, -2.2, -4.6) shows only that math-verify is not the source, not that the drop is real. The caveat is given for the gate but not applied to the loop headline. A boxed-free answer extractor, or accuracy conditional on a boxed answer being present, is needed.

Also raised: Loop decline is not decomposed into format (boxed share) versus mathematical accuracy | Re-scoring with V' and the independent grader do not address the dependence on \boxed, so 'decline in place' is weaker than it reads

comments.title: 'Null' framing sits against a consistent, interval-excluding decline, read asymmetrically
comments.quote:
The
loop does not help; the point estimates are negative in all three seeds, but the
sample is three seeds with one exam draw and one rate, so we do not claim that
it costs accuracy, and we did not isolate the cause.
comments.explanation:
The paper's own t-interval for the mean excludes zero on the negative side for pass@1 and sample accuracy, and the headline calls the result a 'null result'. A decline with an interval excluding zero is not a null; it is a (modest, uncertain-in-cause) negative effect. The hedge is reasonable given n=3, but then the same caution should apply to the language 'null', 'no gain detectable', and to using 'the detectable effect is about 6 points' (computed from a single-seed bootstrap half-width, 2.8h/1.96 with h about 4.2) as the resolution of a three-seed design; the three-seed mean has a different (and by the paper's own interval, smaller) half-width, and the 6-point figure omits seed variance that the paper just measured. Sample-accuracy intervals exclude zero in two of three seeds; 'two intervals exclude zero' for pass@1 is also stated while claiming only absence of benefit.

Also raised: Significant, consistent decline in the final round coexists with a 'null' headline and is treated asymmetrically | Title and framing call the result a 'null' although the final round shows a consistent decline and the positive control fails | Asymmetric reading of consistent declines versus gains; declines are never pooled | Null-for-gains is asserted with no equivalence test while point estimates are consistently negative | Final-round decline is consistent in sign, two graders and the mean interval, yet discussion treats it as 'not detectable'/uninterpreted

comments.title: Detectable-effect (power) figures are optimistic: one-run bootstrap, no seed variance, weakest metric
comments.quote: even with h as the whole error, a gain at that size is missed 20% of the time,
comments.explanation:
The 2.8h/1.96 rule uses the bootstrap half-width of a single run, which omits training-seed variance. The paper's own gauge (replicate pair 3.2 pts apart; B-A flipping +5.3 to -7.3; per-seed sample-accuracy swings of a few points) implies true minimum detectable effects well above 10 pts pass@1, yet the abstract, Intro and Conclusion repeat 'about 10 (6)' as the design's sensitivity, with 'likely more' in small print. The paper criticises others for ignoring seed variance (Xu et al.) but its headline sensitivity does the same; a seed-variance-inclusive estimate (e.g., pooling the 3 seeds at 1e-4 in Table 2 or the 3 final-round seeds) is available and should replace the optimistic figure. Further, pass@1 uses one sample per problem, so its detectability is far worse than that of sample accuracy, which was nevertheless chosen post hoc as primary.

Also raised: Detectable-effect thresholds are optimistic yet presented as the design's sensitivity; seed variance is not estimated | Detectable-effect ('power') claims and 'null for the recipe' are presented as informative although the positive control fails in every configuration | Interval-based claims of decline lean on intervals the paper says are optimistic

comments.title: Seven simultaneous recipe changes and no no-filter arm: the final-round decline cannot be attributed
comments.quote:
Because no earlier arm improved, we ran one last round with several recipe
changes made at once, aimed at the suspected causes (no ablation of any single
one)
comments.explanation:
Completion-only loss, all-linear LoRA, 1,024 cap, normalised gold, a new 300-problem MATH-train pool, k=2, one adapter and LR 1e-4 all change together. Moreover the final round is a single round with selection problems disjoint from the exam, whereas the earlier collapse story (shrinking pool shaped by the biased verifier, selection==eval in Design P) needs multiple rounds and overlap. So the final round cannot confirm or deny any earlier explanation, and a null/negative here is not comparable with Tables 1-3. 'Aimed at suspected causes' is also unsupported: the paper elsewhere says the cause is not identified. Further, the pool of 300 'MATH training split' problems has no overlap check against MATH-500 (stated), which could bias the loop and the gate in either direction, and the paper does not say whether the three seeds redraw the pool.

Also raised: No filter-free/random-data control in the final round: loop decline cannot be separated from generic SFT damage, yet is hedged inconsistently

comments.title: Earlier runs are graded only by the biased selecting verifier; verifier attenuation not carried into thresholds
comments.quote: normalised gold answers, and a pool of 300 problems from
comments.explanation:
Earlier runs are graded by V with the gold-storage defect (which rejects 15-18% of correct answers and zeroes 10% of problems), whereas the final round uses normalised gold and a second string-match grader that reads only the last \boxed. It is unclear whether the gold-storage defect and the 51 unparseable golds persist in the final round; if they were fixed, the final-round round-0 accuracy and selection pool are measured differently from every earlier run (round-0 ~49% on 500 vs ~31-33% on 150), so the 'detectable 6 vs 10 points' and the sign-consistent decline are not comparable to the earlier null. Conversely, if not fixed, selection still has the defect. The paper also never reports whether the independent grader agrees with V at the problem level (only differences), so agreement of aggregate deltas is weak evidence of validity.

Also raised: Measurement attenuation by the verifier is not carried into the detectable-effect claims

comments.title: Injected-bias controls are underpowered and over-read as 'opposite to avoidance'
comments.quote: every \boxed answer is rejected when the gold contains \frac
comments.explanation:
The model sees the problem, not the gold, so the rule is learnable only insofar as problem text predicts a \frac gold. Moreover the control runs a single adapter on 49 penalised problems for one round at k=2, while the real audit spans several rounds, a different dose (2-12 avoidance examples) and a different penalty (a rejected correct answer, not a blanket rule). The negative result (+2.8 in the wrong direction) is thus evidence that this setting does not elicit avoidance at all, which is itself informative about the expected adaptation to the real defect (probably none), yet the paper says both are uninformative and 'expects weak pressure (untested)'. The framing as 'intended positive controls' that 'turn out not to be' is therefore too pessimistic in one place and the audit's detectability remains unquantified in another.

Also raised: Injected-bias interpretations are applied selectively despite being declared uninterpretable | Injected-bias controls have no stated expected effect, and the 'opposite direction' reading rests on an interval containing zero | Abstract claims the injected-bias runs 'show no selective avoidance', but the evidence is too weak to support even that | Injected-bias result is interpreted as 'opposite to avoidance' despite an interval compatible with avoidance and a design that cannot elicit it | Injected-bias runs are too weak to act as positive controls, and the opposite-direction reading overreaches

comments.title: Cap-share decomposition is unstable (-2% to 72%), contradicts Table 2, and is promoted to a headline
comments.quote: attributes 12–30% of the decline to the cap share in the three original seed-1
comments.explanation:
The cap share ranges from -2% to 72% across runs, i.e. the decomposition does not replicate and its sign changes; yet the contribution list and introduction present 'lower accuracy on the solutions the model does finish' as what 'appears most clearly'. A three-part decomposition with an interaction term has an order-dependent apportionment, so the percentages are not uniquely defined. The matched measure conditions on which problems finish post-training (selection into the finished set), which the paper concedes is only descriptive, and the cap-hit proxy (re-tokenised >=508) is approximate. With 40-50% of generations already capped at baseline and 24-26% of training examples truncated of their final answer and EOS, the cap may also be the cause of finished-accuracy loss (training on truncated, answer-less targets), not a separable component. Same-seed A/B pairs are replicates and B-A flips +5.3 to -7.3 from 0-3 example differences, so interval-based claims at problem level understate run-to-run variance.

Also raised: Cap-share range reported selectively in the audit section | Conclusion drops the seed-2 cap-share caveat stated in Intro and Section 4.5 | Cap-share decomposition contradicts the matched-finished column and covers undefined runs | Highlighted accuracy-decline decomposition rests on a result that flips by seed and is stated without uncertainty | Conclusion states finished-accuracy loss flatly despite descriptive/post hoc status | 'Finished accuracy carries the whole change' at lower rates rests on point estimates whose intervals include zero

comments.title: r_t identity: boxed-share fall is the adaptation channel; audit is non-diagnostic yet recommended
comments.quote: an identity, not a test, which does not
comments.explanation:
r_t = r_boxed x (boxed share) is an algebraic decomposition that holds under every hypothesis, adaptation or not, so it cannot 'account for' the fall; it only re-expresses it. Worse, the only way a policy can escape the gold-storage defect on a problem with parseable gold is to stop writing \boxed there, so a falling boxed share is precisely the mechanism by which adaptation would show up. Attributing the fall to the share and then calling it 'no evidence of adaptation' treats the main adaptation route as a nuisance factor. The honest reading is that the data do not identify non-selective unboxing (generic SFT damage, shorter/capped outputs) versus selective avoidance; 'accounted for' overstates, and the evidence is the (weak) r_boxed term, whose intervals (about +-3) contain the whole fall.

Also raised: r_boxed 'flat' is not a usable reference: the gold arm shows r_boxed drifting by as much as the effect | Recommending r_t as a per-round audit contradicts the paper's own finding that it is non-diagnostic | Train-on-gold used as a 'drift' control although its accepted set is collapsed and the effect is opposite in sign | Audit and Table 5: intervals mostly include zero yet drift in the control arm is used to dismiss; no multiplicity across 15 intervals

comments.title: 'Affected, parseable' subset is outcome-defined and counts mix exam and selection problems
comments.quote: problems where some form could, rt moves by −5.5, −1.6 and −0.2 points
comments.explanation:
The subset (problems where the defect 'ever fires') is selected using the same generations in which r_t is later measured; a problem enters only if a boxed correct answer was produced and rejected in some round. This conditioning forces r_t on this subset near its ceiling at round 0 (92-95%) and makes later values fall back by construction (regression to the mean), independent of any learning. Likewise the headline 'rejects 94-98% of correct answers in every round' on problems where it ever fires is a selection-induced rate, not an estimate of the defect's per-problem hit rate. A subset fixed from round 0 only, or from an independent sample, is needed.

Also raised: Affected-problem counts mix exam and selection problems, overstating the adaptive-pressure set | Number of affected parseable problems (24-28) not derivable from 54-62 minus 29-34 | Unparseable-gold problems and partition differences affect fairness of paired/cross-seed comparisons

comments.title: Controls are not dose-matched; no-filter 'lower on pass@k' has intervals including zero
comments.quote: takes 3–4× Run A’s optimizer steps
comments.explanation:
The no-filter arm trains on 1,400 examples versus 326-440 for filtered, and gold on 350, so the three arms differ in steps, truncation rate (62.4% vs 24.5%) and content. The paper then reports 'no filter is lower on pass@k' in the abstract and Discussion, while asserting that it cannot be attributed. A random subsample of the no-filter pool to the filtered size (or a size-matched random selection) would have been a direct, cheap fix and is exactly the 'check the dose first' protocol the paper recommends in 5.3(iii) to others. Since the same lesson was identified post hoc and deferred to 'first thing next', the claim 'removing the filter makes no consistent difference' is neither a null nor a difference; and a no-filter arm is missing altogether from the final round, where the loop declines.

Also raised: No-filter versus filtered comparison: unexplained truncation figures and dose confound | Abstract states controls 'show no consistent difference' while the same sentence reports the no-filter arm is lower | Abstract says no-filter 'is lower on pass@k' though the body shows it is within noise

comments.title: Learning-rate grid conflates rate with k, rounds and metric; dose-response and 1e-5 premise are weak
comments.quote: so only 10−4 to 5 × 10−4 isolates the
comments.explanation:
The 1e-5 arm (k=8, 5 rounds, pass@8) and the 1e-4..5e-4 arms (k=4, 3 rounds, pass@4) differ in more than rate, and the final round changes seven things at once (k=2, 1 adapter, new pool, loss, LoRA targets, cap). pass@k values for different k are not comparable, and pass@1 compares a single draw. Neither is the 1e-5 arm a low-dose match of the higher-rate arms. 'No gain at any learning rate' is thus a union of non-comparable null tests, each with different sensitivity, and the headline sentence reads as a rate sweep that was not performed. The authors state the confound but still headline the conclusion at rate level; moreover the best-case design for finding a gain (more rounds at the intermediate rate with k held fixed) was not run.

Also raised: Dose-response reading from two seeds sits inside the paper's own noise floor | Dose-response reading rests on single runs whose same-seed replicate spread is as large as the effect | Premise that the 1e-5 adapter 'did little' is contradicted by Run C at the same rate | Selection step and training-data construction under-described; 1e-5 'default' rate gives a near-null intervention

comments.title: Pooled-vs-isolated confound list is incomplete; 'apparent collapse' framing unsupported
comments.quote: decline is absent in the isolated runs at 10−5,
comments.explanation:
The paper names dose and pooling, but Design P also differs in: evaluation on the selection problems themselves (selection == eval, so lost problems drop out of the pool and the pool shrinks as a function of what is evaluated), no held-out set, two datasets with very different solution lengths (Run C alone declines 12.7), a 0.5B/1.5B pair, and an accelerating pool-shrinkage feedback that the isolated runs, with a separate exam, cannot reproduce. Isolated runs do decline (pass@1 -2.7 to -12.7 at 1e-5, up to -22 on GSM8K at 5e-4), so 'absent' is a statement about magnitude only. The shrinking-pool hypothesis is also said to be neither supported nor ruled out, yet the no-filter arm (constant pool) declines too, which actually argues the shrinkage is not necessary for decline. No dose-matched isolated run exists (they could have trained Run A at 5e-4 for 5 rounds on the pooled dose), so the confound is never reduced.

Also raised: Pooled-design 'collapse' framed as apparent, with unsupported 'acceleration' and without noting that selection equals evaluation

comments.title: No multiplicity handling; bootstrap details missing
comments.quote: We make no multiplicity correction and the runs are not independent (they share
comments.explanation:
The central claim 'No pass@1 or pass@k gain has an interval excluding zero' is effectively an intersection null over ~20 runs x 4 metrics, while many cells share exam partitions and round-0 draws. Not correcting is conservative for a claim of 'no gain' (it makes false positives more likely), but the paper then uses uncorrected 95% intervals to highlight subsets that do exclude zero (5e-4 decline in 'four A/B runs', 'five of six' matched intervals) and builds the 'lower accuracy on finished solutions' headline on them. The treatment is inconsistent: multiplicity is waved away in the null direction yet the same uncorrected intervals support the one positive claim in the abstract/Introduction. The 'descriptive not tests' disclaimer does not stop these being headline claims.

Also raised: Bootstrap and inference procedure details missing; multiple-comparison stance cuts one way

comments.title: Probe false-negative rate, defect rate and r_t denominators are not reconciled; 'directional bias' asserted
comments.quote: inspected only rejections; the gold-storage defect ran unvaried through every
comments.explanation:
The probe finds a 7.8% false-negative rate (10/128, on Qwen2.5-7B solutions) and attributes most of it to the gold-storage defect, but the same defect is later said to reject 15.5-18.3% of what V' accepts in the 1.5B loop, plus 10.2% of golds are unparseable. The two figures differ by about 2x, and the 128 vs 200 sample is restricted to 'judged correct by a scripted normalised comparison', so the audit may under- or over-state the 1.5B loop. Moreover the audit 'inspected only rejections, so it gives no false-positive rate', and Section 4.4 says its checks bound verifier error 'from below only'. For a paper whose second question is whether the model learns what the selecting verifier accepts, an unbounded false-positive rate and self-grading by that verifier (Limitations: headline numbers are graded by the same verifier) mean the Conclusion's 'neither branch is answered' is appropriate, but the Intro's and Section 4.4's 'we think this fall is unlikely to be mainly veriﬁer error' is not supported.

Also raised: Probe false-negative rate (7.8%) is not reconciled with the loop-level rejection rate (15.5-18.3%) | Denominators of the defect/false-reject statistics (r_t) are unclear and not reconciled | 'About one in six' / 15.5-18.3% is a self-training-only figure; Table 5 gold rows exceed it and the range mixes round 0 with last round | 'Directional bias' is asserted although only false rejections were measured

comments.title: Harness integration defect generalised to rule-based verifiers; scope caveats absent from the abstract
comments.quote: so a correct boxed prediction can fail against a bare gold
comments.explanation:
The dominant defect arises because the authors store the gold without delimiters; math-verify used as documented (gold parsed with delimiters) would not exhibit it, and V' is simply the correct call. The 29-34 of 54-62 affected problems with unparseable gold are a different cause (parser limits) folded into the same count. The title question ('Mathematics or the Verifier?'), the RLVR framing, and the claim that bias in 'a rule-based verifier' was studied overreach: the experiment shows what a mis-wired pipeline does, not what verifier bias does. The 4.7-8.0 point pass@1 'cost' is a scoring artefact of the defect, not evidence of biased selection pressure, and V' itself has no false-accept check (only rejections were audited).

Also raised: Scope caveats (instruct-tuned, one model/verifier, contamination) are not reflected in Abstract or Conclusion generalisation

comments.title: 512-token cap and repetition penalty depress the baseline; truncation mitigation has no numbers
comments.quote: Retraining without truncated examples, or re-scoring at a 1,536-token cap
comments.explanation:
Section 3.4 says 24-26% of the round-0 pool (62.4% for no-filter) is cut in training and so loses its final answer and end-of-sequence token; this directly teaches the model not to finish, the very effect (cap-hit share rising, 40-46% of generations hitting the cap even at round 0) that the paper later decomposes. The only mitigation, 'leaves the deficit in place', is given with no rates, seeds, numbers or counts and is deferred to Supplementary Appendix H, while the Code availability paragraph admits 'the 1,536-token re-scoring outputs were not saved'. The claim therefore cannot be checked from the paper or the released artefacts. The Limitations merely list 'Truncation: the 512-token cap binds from the start' and do not tie it to the headline null (a gain via learning to finish within 512 tokens is the most plausible first-order effect of this filter, and is exactly what the setup can mask or reverse). Also unclear is whether the 'retraining without truncated examples' used the same runs/rates.

Also raised: Baseline is depressed by a 512-token cap and repetition penalty; the caveat is one clause in Limitations and is not carried to the headline | The 512-token cap binds for ~43% of baseline generations, so the loop's selector is also a length filter | Matched finished-accuracy measure and cap-hit threshold are underspecified

comments.title: Sensitivity figures conflict: 3.5-5.5 detectable vs 'about 2.2' bound that matches no interval
comments.quote: is the largest upper limit among observed intervals
comments.explanation:
Section 3.4 says sample-accuracy gains below about 3.5-5.5 points could be missed; Section 5.1 reports a ~2.2-point figure that is the maximum of the upper limits of observed intervals. The latter is a maximum over a selected, post hoc statistic across non-independent runs, not a bound on any effect; its natural reading ('gains above 2.2 are excluded') contradicts the 3.5-5.5 detectability threshold stated earlier. Using a max-of-upper-limits is also a form of selecting the most favourable summary and, as intervals omit seed variance, understates uncertainty. It should either be removed or reconciled with the power statement.

Also raised: 'About 2.2 points' sample-accuracy bound does not correspond to any interval in the final round and is described ambiguously | Sample-accuracy detectability stated as 3.5-5.5 points in the Introduction but as ~2.2 points in Section 5.1 | The '2.2-point bound' and 'about 2 points' verifier bound are confusable and conflict with the stated 3.5-5.5 detectability | 'About 2.2 points' as an upper limit on gains is a maximum over runs, not a bound

comments.title: n=3 t-interval is fragile and the seed spread is mostly round-0 sampling noise
comments.quote:
The mean pass@1 change over the three seeds is
−4.1 (t interval [−6.1, −2.1]), and −4.5 for sample accuracy ([−8.1, −1.0]).
comments.explanation:
Arithmetic checks out: mean -4.07, sd 0.81, t(2)=4.30 gives [-6.1,-2.1]; sample accuracy likewise gives [-8.05,-1.0]. But the interval rests on two degrees of freedom, so its width is dominated by an sd estimated from three points (pass@1 sd 0.8 vs per-seed bootstrap half-widths of about 4, an implausibly small ratio that is probably luck). All seeds share the same 500 exam problems (and probably the same 300 pool; unspecified), so the interval covers loop/sampling randomness only, not problem-draw variance; it cannot support a population-level claim about the recipe. The post-training pass@1 values are 44.4, 43.6, 44.0, a tight cluster while round-0 pass@1 varies 46.8-49.2 from sampling noise alone, so part of the 'seed' variance in the change is baseline sampling noise. A sign test over three seeds (p=0.125 one-sided) is not significant. Nine intervals are examined (3 metrics x 3 seeds) with no multiplicity correction.

Also raised: Round-0 sampling noise drives the spread of per-seed final-round changes | Round-0 baselines and comparisons: untrained rows differ per seed and the gate has one seed against a single baseline

comments.title: 'Seed' semantics contradict the fixed trainer seed 42
comments.quote: gradient clipping 1.0 and trainer seed 42
comments.explanation: Section 3.3 defines a seed as setting the exam partition, selection set and training randomness at once, and 3.4 says Python and torch seeds are set from the run seed. But the trainer seed is listed as fixed at 42. In HF Trainer/TRL the trainer seed calls set_seed at initialisation and controls data shuffling (and any init performed after it), so it can override the run-seed torch seeding and make data order identical across 'seeds'. If so, what is called seed variation is mostly partition variation, the 'replicate' gauge and the 3-seed t-intervals do not measure training variance as claimed, and the statement 'which we see only across two or three seeds' is not accurate. The paper should state which RNGs (LoRA init, data order, sampling) actually vary with the run seed.

comments.title: pass@1 is a single draw and the primary metric was switched after the runs
comments.quote: so after the runs we chose it as the primary accuracy measure.
comments.explanation:
pass@1 is defined as correctness of the first of k samples, a single Bernoulli draw per problem. The standard pass@1 (Chen et al.) is the expected single-sample accuracy, which here is exactly the 'sample accuracy' mean over k samples. The preregistered metric is therefore a deliberately noisy estimator of the quantity of interest, which is why its detectable effect is about 10 points, and the headline 'no pass@1 gain detectable' is largely a property of that choice. The more sensitive measure was then adopted after seeing results, and Section 4.4 and later claims about declines ('intervals exclude zero in all four A/B runs') rest on it while the pre-set pass@1 intervals mostly include zero. The disclosure is honest, but the post hoc switch is unequal to the standard applied elsewhere (no multiplicity correction yet decline claims read off the metric that gives exclusion), and 'pass@1' should be renamed (e.g. single-draw accuracy) to avoid confusion with the usual metric. The '2.2-point bound' mentioned here is also not defined in this section.

Also raised: Primary measure is inconsistent: sample accuracy declared primary but headlines, detectable effect and abstract use pass@1

comments.title: Key claims rest only on appendices; some cross-references do not resolve
comments.quote: (24–26% of the round-0 pool; Section 4.5)
comments.explanation:
Section 3.4 sends the reader to Section 4.5 for the 24-26% truncated share of the round-0 pool, but Section 4.5 contains no such figure (the 24.5% vs 62.4% appears in Section 4.4 and the 24-26% only here). Section 5.1 cites 're-scoring ﬁve runs ... Section 3' (the analysis is 3.2 and Appendix B), the 1e-5 default is 'not tuned (Section 4.4)' though 4.4 only motivates higher rates, and the Conclusion says 'a second grader come ﬁrst (Supplementary Appendix K)' although a string-match second grader was already used in Section 5.1 (presumably a different, e.g. model-based, grader is meant, which is not stated). These make it hard to check claims against their evidence.

Also raised: Key supporting analyses are only in unseen appendices with no numbers in the main text

comments.title: Table 2 value for B seed 1 at 1e-5 is stale versus the recomputed B-A
comments.quote: (recomputed from the saved generations; Table 2 lists run-log values, −0.7 at seed 1)
comments.explanation:
Section 4.3 says that the recomputed B-A difference at seed 1 is +0.0, whereas Table 2 gives -4.0 for B,1 and -3.3 for A,1 (difference -0.7). So at least one pass@1 entry in Table 2 is a run-log value that differs from the recomputed one. The Table 2 caption, however, says that only six round values differ by one problem, and gives a pass@8 example, without flagging this pass@1 entry. Section 4.2 then reports 'pass@1 is 2.7-4.0 points lower at round 4', where 4.0 comes from the stale B,1 entry. With recomputed values the range would be 2.7-3.3. The table intervals are bootstrapped on recomputed generations while the point estimate is from the log, so the interval might not be centred on the printed estimate. The table should use one source for all columns, and the caption should state which cells are affected.

Also raised: Table 2 point estimate for B at seed 1 conflicts with the recomputed B-A difference

comments.title: Number of examples changed by the \dfrac patch is given as 3-4, 0-3 and 0-4
comments.quote: the patch changes 0–4 training examples
comments.explanation:
Section 4.3 says kept pools differ by '3-4 examples (under 0.5% of the 872-example pool)'; Section 4.4 says pools differ 'by 0-3 examples' for the seed-flip comparison; Section 3.2, Limitations and 5.3 say '0-4'. These can be different runs, but the text does not say so, and the point (B-A flipping +5.3 to -7.3 on 'near-identical pools') depends on the pool difference for those runs. Specify the pool difference per run pair.

Also raised: Patch specification and its effect size are ambiguous

comments.title: Cap-hit ranges quoted in text do not match Table 1
comments.quote: 40–46% of round-2 MATH-500
comments.explanation: Section 4.5 says 'at the rates where the share does not rise, 40-46%' of round-2 generations hit the cap, but Table 1 lists 39.7% for 2x10^-4 seed 2 (range is 39.7-45.7). It also says the cap-hit share 'rises 2-14 points' at 5x10^-4, while Table 1 gives rises of only 3.2 (43.0->46.2) and 8.0 (43.2->51.2) for the A runs; the 14 must come from B/no-filter runs shown only in supplementary Table S9. The decomposition percentages (12-30%, 52-72%) cannot be checked from the main text. Minor, but these are the numbers the decomposition rests on.

comments.title: 3.2-point replicate gauge is not derivable from reported pairs
comments.quote: the replicate pair we use as a gauge ends 3.2 points of sample accuracy apart
comments.explanation: The 3.2 gauge is used twice (3.4, and in the argument that thresholds are 'optimistic') to bound training-seed variance. The only same-configuration pairs in Table 2 are A (seed 0 vs 1): sample-accuracy change -2.4 vs -1.5 (diff 0.9), B: -3.2 vs -1.2 (diff 2.0), 1e-4 seeds -1.5/-3.7/-1.0 (range 2.7), 2e-4 -3.5/-3.8, 5e-4 -8.3/-4.7. None gives 3.2 as a change difference. If 3.2 is a difference in levels (not changes) it mixes partition variance, as the text admits, but then it is not a measure of training variance, and the final-round loop (same exam, three seeds) shows round-1 values within 0.8 points. Identify the pair and the quantity.

comments.title: Units of 'problems added/lost' in Table 1 versus pool sizes in Table 3
comments.quote: problems added/lost summed over rounds 1–2
comments.explanation: Table 1 gives added/lost of 22/33 for A at seed 1 (5e-4), a net of -11, while Table 3 shows the kept pool falling from 440 to 326 examples (-114). For seed 2 the net is -10 against 424 to 350 (-74). The two quantities are probably in different units (distinct problems vs. examples, with several accepted samples per problem), but this is not said. The number of distinct accepted problems is also not reported, so it is unclear how much of the drop in pool size comes from fewer problems solved and how much from fewer solved samples per problem. Because pool contraction is central to the 'self-reinforcing shrinking pool' reading in 5.2, the units need to be stated.

comments.title: Independent-grader changes are given without intervals
comments.quote: changes of −3.6, −2.2, −4.6 for the three seeds
comments.explanation: The abstract, Discussion and Conclusion headline 'pass@1 falls 3.2-4.8 points in each of three seeds' (verifier-graded). The independent grader, the only non-verifier check, gives -3.6, -2.2, -4.6 (mean -3.47, range 2.2-4.6) and sample-accuracy -2.5, -5.5, -5.3, with no intervals reported. Seed 2 is -2.2 under the string grader versus an already-zero-touching [-6.8,+0.6] interval under the verifier (-3.2), so under the independent grader at least that seed very likely includes zero, and the 't interval' and the 'two of three exclude zero' claim are not reproduced for the second grader. 'Same sign and size' hides that the independent range (2.2-4.6) and mean (-3.5) are lower than the quoted -4.1. Report intervals and the mean/t-interval under the independent grader.

comments.title: Boxed-only interval width stated as about +-3 though one run is about +-1.6
comments.quote: have intervals (≈±3) that contain the overall fall of the same run (−2.6, −2.6,
comments.explanation: Table 5 boxed-only intervals are [-2.9,4.3], [-2.8,3.4] and [-2.0,1.2], i.e. half-widths about 3.6, 3.1 and 1.6. For the 1e-5 run the 'flat means not detected' argument rests on an interval whose half-width is half that stated, and the overall fall (-1.5, [-2.9,0.0]) is nearly outside it. Minor, but 'flat means not detected' should be run-specific. Also the overall-fall intervals touch zero, so the comparison 'interval contains the overall fall' does not establish equivalence.

comments.title: No train/exam overlap check for the 300-problem MATH-train pool
comments.quote: We report no overlap check of the 300 pool problems
comments.explanation: The final-round pool is 300 MATH training problems evaluated on all MATH-500. No overlap or near-duplicate check is reported, and the Limitations section (which lists contamination of Qwen2.5 on MATH/GSM8K) omits this item. Overlap would inflate loop and gate accuracy in the final round, which is the paper's strongest evidence round; it should be checked or listed.

comments.title: Status of gold normalisation in the final round is unclear
comments.quote: no run varies the frequent gold-storage defect
comments.explanation: Section 4.6 lists 'normalised gold answers' among the seven simultaneous recipe changes, and the Abstract says 'Scores before the ﬁnal round use the veriﬁer with the defect', implying the final round does not. If normalisation removes the defect (a bare-gold problem), then the final round does vary it, in conflict with this sentence and with the Limitations, and it is confounded with six other changes, so the second branch (does it learn the verifier's style) has some evidence the paper does not use; if it does not, the Abstract sentence is wrong. The text never says whether the selecting verifier and the exam verifier in 4.6 still store the gold bare, whether the 298/263 kept counts and the injected-bias runs are under V or V', or whether Table 5's audit could be applied to the final round. This cannot be resolved from the paper.

comments.title: Related-work differentiator and Kim et al. analogy are not supported by the paper's own findings
comments.quote: does to the training pool, not only
comments.explanation:
Related Work distinguishes the paper from Xu et al. by 'auditing what that verifier's filtering does to the training pool, not only whether accuracy moved'. The audit is described in the abstract, the Introduction and Section 5.3 as uninformative about adaptation. Its fall is an identity with the boxed share, its subsets have intervals of 10-26 points, the pool holds only 2-12 relevant examples, and no valid positive control exists. The same Related Work paragraph then says the measurement is 'not new' and that the paper 'claims neither it nor the patch control as a contribution'. Presenting the audit as a point of difference and also as a non-contribution is inconsistent. The 'rejection defect we measured' also rests on another model's solutions (Qwen2.5-7B, 200 problems, 128 judged correct), as the limitations say. The difference from prior work is therefore smaller than the framing suggests.

Also raised: Analogy to Kim et al. self-distillation is offered for train-on-gold collapse without a matching mechanism
